questions.text: The formula y ~ x1 * x2 expands to which set of terms?
options: x1, x2, and x1:x2 (the interaction term)
x1, x2, x1:x2, and an additional x1^2:x2 term
questions.explanation: y ~ x1 * x2 is shorthand for y ~ x1 + x2 + x1:x2 — main effects for x1 and x2 plus their interaction term.

questions.text: In an additive model y ~ x1 + x2 (with x2 categorical), the slope of x1 is the same for all levels of x2.
questions.explanation: The additive model allows different intercepts per group (via dummy variables) but forces a single shared slope for x1. Only the interaction model (y ~ x1 * x2) allows slopes to differ by group.

questions.text: You fit both additive and interaction models. The residual plot for the additive model shows a strong colour gradient (coloured by the grouping variable x2). This indicates:
options: The slopes of x1 differ by group — the interaction term is needed
The intercepts are identical across groups
There are influential outliers in the data
questions.explanation: A colour gradient in residuals (where colour encodes group) means the additive model's single shared slope is wrong for some groups. The interaction term would allow different slopes per group.

questions.text: You want to fit a model with log(y) as the response and x as the predictor. Which formula is correct?
questions.explanation: In R, transformations of the response are written directly in the formula: lm(log(y) ~ x). R evaluates log(y) before fitting. lm(y ~ log(x)) would instead transform the predictor.

questions.text: Which code correctly creates a quadratic term for x in an lm() formula?
questions.explanation: poly(x, 2, raw=TRUE) creates ordinary polynomial terms x and x². Using I(x^2) also works. y ~ x^2 is a formula crossing operator and collapses to y ~ x.
